title: India Lifts Emergency Fuel Restrictions Starting July 1 as Oil Prices Collapse
excerpt: The 200-litre diesel cap and ban on commercial buyers at retail pumps are gone. Brent crude has fallen 42% from its April peak, and windfall taxes are being reshuffled.
body:
India will lift all emergency restrictions on petrol and diesel sales at retail fuel stations starting July 1, the government announced on Monday, marking the end of a turbulent three-week period in which a war in the Middle East forced New Delhi to ration fuel for the first time in years.

The Oil and Natural Gas Ministry said it had reviewed the supply situation and concluded that the restrictions were “no longer necessary in the public interest.” The order withdraws the June 12 directive that had capped diesel purchases at 200 litres per customer per day and barred industrial, commercial, and institutional buyers from purchasing fuel at retail outlets operated by public sector oil marketing companies.

The restrictions were imposed after the conflict between the US and Iran — raging since February 28 — disrupted global supply chains. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz hit India particularly hard: the country imports 85 per cent of its crude oil, 50 per cent of its LNG, and 60 per cent of its LPG. When international prices spiked, the government shielded retail consumers by holding domestic fuel prices steady, creating a gap of roughly ₹40 per litre between retail and bulk diesel. Commercial buyers flooded retail stations to exploit the difference, causing hoarding, black marketing, and panic buying in some districts.

## How Bad Did It Get?

The numbers were stark. Private oil marketing companies saw a 58 per cent decline in diesel sales during May 2026 as their higher prices drove customers to PSU pumps instead. Across 327 districts, PSU retail outlets recorded more than 10 per cent growth in diesel sales over the same period last year; 80 districts saw surges exceeding 30 per cent. Bulk industrial and commercial users diverted an estimated 3.5 lakh tonnes of diesel through retail outlets in May alone.

The restrictions hit hardest in the transport and agriculture sectors. Farmers in the midst of kharif season struggled to fuel irrigation pumps and farm machinery. Small and medium enterprises that run on diesel faced operational disruptions. The 200-litre daily cap, while preventing hoarding, created logistical headaches for trucking operators and construction firms.

## The Oil Price Collapse That Changed Everything

What ultimately made the restrictions unnecessary was a dramatic collapse in oil prices. Brent crude has fallen 42 per cent from its April peak of $126.4 per barrel to around $73, retreating to levels seen before the Iran conflict. The US-Iran interim peace deal and the 60-day sanctions reprieve that followed — allowing Iran to resume crude oil and refined product exports — restored shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz and eased supply fears.

The government had already signalled normalisation last week by lifting all restrictions on LPG supply to commercial and industrial users.

## Windfall Taxes Reshuffled

Alongside the fuel curb reversal, India has also recalibrated its windfall taxes on petroleum exports effective July 1. The export duty on diesel has been slashed from ₹14 to ₹8.5 per litre, and aviation turbine fuel duty has been cut from ₹12.5 to ₹7.5 per litre. In the other direction, the petrol export duty has been raised from ₹1.5 to ₹4 per litre to ensure domestic supply.

Economists forecast Brent crude will average $84.50 per barrel in 2026, down from the $90.44 projected last month. Goldman Sachs has raised its 2026 India growth forecast by 30 basis points on the back of improved energy dynamics.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs with family or business interests in India, the fuel episode offers both relief and a reminder. The restrictions disrupted ground-level commerce — from trucking to farming to MSMEs — in ways that rippled through supply chains. NRI-owned businesses in transport and manufacturing were among those affected.

The broader takeaway is about India’s energy vulnerability. Despite maintaining stable retail prices throughout the crisis, the episode exposed how dependent the economy remains on imported oil and how quickly a Middle East conflict can cascade into fuel rationing at the neighbourhood pump. With Brent at $73 and the rupee posting its first quarterly gain since March 2025, the pressure has eased — for now.
